content:
Apple has filed a new document in its ongoing lawsuit against OpenAI, continuing to push for expedited discovery. In today's filing, Apple says it has obtained new "stunning evidence" based on preliminary forensic analysis of the laptop used by former engineer Chang Liu.

Apple first filed the lawsuit in July of this year, alleging a former employee stole trade secrets to benefit OpenAI. Several weeks later, Apple filed for a preliminary injunction while also requesting that the court expedite discovery, including requesting early document production and deposition of key OpenAI employees and executives. Apple reiterated the urgency of expedited discovery last week. OpenAI has asked the court to dismiss the case.

As previously reported, Chang Liu is one of the defendants named in Apple's lawsuit. Liu was a senior systems hardware engineer at Apple who left to join OpenAI in January. The lawsuit alleges that Liu exploited a security vulnerability to download confidential engineering files after his departure.

In today's filing, Apple says Liu's attorneys recently turned over a MacBook he used after leaving Apple. Apple says the "preliminary forensic analysis" of the MacBook revealed four things, quoted directly from Apple's filing:

  • Not only did Mr. Liu download a confidential Apple schematic, but he used it in his work at OpenAI;
  • Mr. Liu was fully aware of his unauthorized access to Apple's third-party cloud storage, and Mr. Liu and others at OpenAI were fully aware of such access;
  • After becoming aware of Apple's internal investigation into him, Mr. Liu instructed an OpenAI colleague to destroy evidence, which the colleague confirmed they would do; and
  • Mr. Liu used a tool with the same name as an Apple internal engineering application in his work at OpenAI, a tool that is used for Apple development work.

Apple says that in March, Liu used LTspice, a hardware engineering tool, to run simulations using the schematic file. In messages around the same time, Liu said that his AI "agent" had learned to run LTspice and review the results.

Apple argues that when trade secrets are fed to AI agents or models that learn from them, that process can "result in irreversible and expanding use of trade secrets."

Apple says that rather than examine the laptop, the defendants have instead chosen to "push a narrative that the device data rebuts the allegations."

Additionally, Apple learned that Liu used the schematic because he opened it on a Mac mini, which synced the file to the MacBook he took from Apple via iCloud. Apple is now seeking access to that Mac mini as well.
